title: Box Factory
subtitle: A minimalist 2D factory-automation game with a full tech tree, save system and endgame, built from code and data.
summary: A Factorio-inspired logistics game: mine ore, belt it through smelters and assemblers, craft science packs, research new tech and activate the Portal to win. Fully data-driven.
about: Box Factory is a Factorio-inspired logistics game. Mine raw ore, belt it to smelters, presses and assemblers, then craft four tiers of science packs from multi-ingredient recipes. Feed those packs to research labs to unlock faster machines, and finally build a Portal and deliver Portal Cores and Focus Crystals to win. Machines are simple colored squares, so the focus stays on systems design and clean, data-driven code.
intro: I wanted to build the core loop of a factory game from scratch and keep it fully data-driven: new items, recipes, buildings and technologies are just ScriptableObject assets, with no code changes required. The goal was a clean architecture that scales to hundreds of moving items without hitching, plus the surrounding pieces a real game needs: a tutorial, main menu, save slots and a win condition.

features.title: Grid & Multi-Cell Footprints
features.text: A central `GridManager` registers which building occupies each cell. A `Footprint` helper handles buildings larger than 1×1 (the 1×2 Splitter, 2×2 Fabricator and 3×3 Portal): sizes are defined as length-along-facing by width-across, so rotating a building automatically rotates its footprint, anchor and output cell.

features.title: Conveyor Transport, Auto-Connect & Animated Belts
features.text: Items travel across each building from an entry point to an exit edge, then hand off to the next building if it has room, so full belts naturally back up. When you place or delete belts, neighbours re-aim themselves so lines connect without manual rotation, with loop checks to avoid feeding a belt into itself. Belt art is a sprite sheet sliced at runtime; chevrons scroll at exactly the item travel speed from one shared clock, and tiles turn into curved corners when fed from the side.

features.title: Miners, Processors & Splitters
features.text: Machine types share one `FactoryBuilding` base class. Miners generate a player-selected ore. Processors run multi-input, multi-output recipes (for example Gear + Copper Wire → Automation Pack), with a Factorio-style recipe picker, input buffers and a live flow diagram. Splitters have two lanes and alternate outputs, falling back to whichever side is free. Settings can be copied and pasted between machines.

features.title: Research, Science Packs & the Portal
features.text: A 14-node tech tree lists prerequisites, item costs and the buildings each tech unlocks. Early techs cost raw items; later ones need Automation, Logistics, Chemical and Quantum packs. Research Labs only accept items the active tech still needs, so everything else blocks on the belt. The endgame Portal accepts Portal Cores and Focus Crystals, shows charging progress and triggers a win screen.

features.title: Save System, Menus & Tutorial
features.text: A main menu, pause menu and slot picker are built entirely in code, with three manual save slots plus a timed autosave. Saves are JSON and reference buildings and items by stable IDs (B01, I01...), so renaming an asset never breaks a save. Machine state is captured too: items in transit, recipe progress, input buffers, research progress, hotbar and camera. A step-by-step tutorial detects when the player completes each action.

features.title: Code-Built, Factorio-Style UI
features.text: The entire HUD is generated at runtime: research readout, a 9-slot hotbar, a categorized build menu, a tech window and a per-machine inspector. Buildings can be dragged from the menu onto hotbar slots. Colors, sizes, fonts and texts come from a `UITheme` asset, so the look can be tweaked without touching code.

features.title: Custom Editor Tooling
features.text: A Content Editor window creates and links items, recipes, buildings and techs with checkbox dropdowns, previews the UI with live mock-ups and validates the whole project (unreachable techs, duplicate IDs, recipe conflicts). A one-click Progression Builder generates the science packs, recipes, prefabs and tech tree, then simulates a full playthrough to prove the game is completable. An ID assigner hands out unique IDs automatically.

features.title: Placement, Drag-Build & Hold-to-Delete
features.text: A snapping ghost preview shows green or red validity, 1×1 buildings can be drag-placed in a line, R rotates the ghost or the hovered building, and holding right-click fills a red overlay on the target before demolishing it.

features.title: Pooling & Procedural Visuals
features.text: Item visuals and particle bursts use Unity's `ObjectPool` under a shared `DontDestroyOnLoad` root. Buildings and items are one generated white square tinted per definition, so the game needs almost no art assets.

notes: Data-driven design: `ItemDefinition`, `RecipeDefinition`, `BuildingDefinition` and `TechDefinition` are ScriptableObjects, so content is added from the editor with no new code.

Items and buildings inherit from `GameDefinition` and get stable IDs, so save files survive asset renames. A `DefinitionRegistry` resolves IDs at load time and still understands legacy name-based saves.
Upgrades are modelled as separate building definitions with higher `speedMultiplier` values (Mk1 to Mk3), unlocked through research, rather than in-place upgrade logic.

Singleton managers (Grid, Research, Build, UI, Save) communicate through C# events like `OnResearchChanged` and `OnTechCompleted`, and bootstrap themselves through `RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod`, so no manual scene wiring is needed.
Uses Unity's new Input System, with UI drag-and-drop built on `EventTrigger` and layout groups generated entirely in code.
Hot paths avoid per-frame allocations: pooled visuals and particles, reused cell lists and cached sprites.
learned: Getting multi-cell buildings to rotate cleanly was the hardest problem. My first approach stored absolute cells, which broke on rotation. Moving to a facing-relative footprint with a center-cell anchor fixed placement, ghost preview and rotation all at once. Adding multi-input recipes and save/load later showed the value of the data-driven design: stable IDs and a registry meant I could rework the economy into a science-pack progression without breaking old saves. Building the UI in code taught me layout groups and event handling in depth, but I'd move to prefab-based UI next time to make iteration faster. Next I'd add power or fuel, ore patches on the map and a belt-lane system for higher throughput.
